Every box tracks `:stable` and Podman updates it. That is the rule for all four
products, and it is why no unit here pins a release number: a box pinned to
`4.17.0` is exactly as old as the day somebody installed it, and nobody goes
back to a plant floor to bump a tag. `release.yml` moves `:stable` on every
tag, and `.github/scripts/release_guard.sh` refuses a release whose units
don't follow it.

Turn the timer on once per box:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
```

## What an update does

Podman pulls `:stable` when the timer fires, and if the digest changed it
restarts the app's unit on the new image. Only the app's: the database
container isn't touched, so an update doesn't bounce the historian. The unit has a healthcheck that
needs no shell (the image has none): `hotloop healthcheck` asks the app's own
`/readyz`, which answers only while the database does. The unit stays in
"activating" until it passes, so Podman can tell an update that came back from
one that didn't, and if the new image never comes up it puts the previous one
back under `:stable` and starts that.

Starting the new image runs its migrations first, on the database that is
already there, and a big database takes a while. The unit gives the app 15
minutes to answer before it calls the update failed, and failures during the
first five minutes don't count, because a migration is not a failure.

Two things were found by running it, not by reading about it, and the units
carry the fix for each. A plain `HealthCmd` string is run through `/bin/sh -c`,
and the image has no shell, so the check could never pass: it is a JSON array.
And older Quadlet reads `Notify=healthy` as plain `true` and passes
`--sdnotify=conmon`, which calls the app up the moment its container starts:
an update that cannot start was reported as a success and nothing was rolled
back. The units say `--sdnotify=healthy` themselves.

## Why there is no pod

The app and the database used to share a pod. That cost the rollback, and it was
found by running it, not by reading the manual. For a container in a pod,
Podman's auto-update restarts the **pod's** unit, and the pod's unit comes up
fine whatever is wrong with the app inside it. A release that couldn't start
was reported as `UPDATED true`, the app crash-looped on it (twenty restarts in
the first minutes), and `:stable` on the box was the broken image. It also
restarted the database on every app update. With a network instead, the app is
its own unit, Podman restarts that, and the unit stays "activating" until the
app answers `/readyz`: the same release came back as `UPDATED rolled back`.

## What a rollback can't undo

A migration. When a release migrates the database and then fails its health
check, Podman puts the previous release back, and it starts on the schema the
failed one left. That is safe, and it is held safe three ways
([MIGRATIONS.md](/iot/migrations/) has the detail):

- **Migrations only add.** A table, a column with a default, an index. Never a
  drop, a rename or a type change, so the previous release finds everything it
  knew where it was and never looks at what was added. A test
  (`TestMigrationsAreAdditive`) fails the build on one that doesn't.
- **The previous release is run on it before a release ships.**
  `test/prevrelease.sh` migrates a database with the new code, then starts the
  last published image on it and runs login, devices, tags, a write through the
  gate and history. It is a step in the release checklist.
- **An app refuses a schema it can't be trusted on.** The database records
  which release applied each migration. A rolled-back release one step behind
  starts, and says so in its log. One two or more releases behind does not
  start and says why, naming both versions. This is the case where a box fails
  an update, rolls back, fails another, and the database has now moved twice.
  The app exits at once with the message in `journalctl -u hotloop`, and the
  unit's `Restart=always` keeps trying and keeps being refused. What fixes it
  is a release that knows the schema: the newest one, which is what `:stable`
  is (`sudo podman auto-update`, or pull it and restart). Or restore a backup
  taken by the release you are on ([BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/)).

So a rollback no longer has a release-notes caveat. What it still can't undo is
data: the failed release may have written rows the old one ignores. Take a
backup before you turn updates on; it is the one thing between a bad release
and a restore.

## Why the database does not follow `:stable`

The app is labeled for auto-update. The database container is not, and its
`Image=` is an exact tag. The reason is that the app's updates can be undone
and the database's can't.

- A **PostgreSQL major version** (16 to 17) is not a restart. PostgreSQL's
  versioning policy says the data directory can't be kept backward compatible
  across majors, and a dump and reload, or `pg_upgrade`, is required
  ([postgresql.org/support/versioning](https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/)).
  A tag that floated across majors would do it to a plant's historian during an
  unrelated restart. Pinning the major is the minimum, and not an "endpoint
  pin" in the sense the rule above is about. The one move HotLoop has made, 16
  to 17, is `hotloop-db-upgrade.container`, run on purpose when you copy the
  new units in.
- A **minor release** (16.14 to 16.15) needs no dump and restore. The same page
  adds that some "might require additional steps so always read the release
  notes first". An unattended box doesn't read release notes.
- **TimescaleDB** (the Gateway and Edge) is the other half. The app runs
  `ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE` itself at startup after a newer image,
  and an extension update is a one-way change to the database: putting the
  older image back afterward doesn't undo it. So a floating Timescale tag would
  make the app's reversible update drag an irreversible one along behind it.
- A new database image that starts and runs is not a healthy one. The
  healthcheck can tell a container that won't start from one that will, and
  that is all it can tell. Whether a historian survived an engine upgrade is
  not something `pg_isready` answers.

So the database tag moves with a HotLoop release that was tested against it.
`release_guard.sh` holds each `hotloop-db.container` equal to its chart's
database, so a Quadlet box and a chart install of the same product run the same
one, and refuses an `AutoUpdate=` on it. The cost is that PostgreSQL's own patch
releases reach a box when a release ships them, or when you change the tag by
hand. Within the same major that is an edit to `hotloop-db.container`, a
`daemon-reload` and a restart of the pod, after reading the release notes and
taking a backup. A major version is `pg_upgrade`, which HotLoop runs for 16 to 17 and which you
run yourself, or restore into, for any other.

## Holding updates until you say

The default is no hold: updates happen when the timer fires. A site that
wants a person to decide has two ways, neither of which needs the app to be
reachable.

- **Hold.** Leave `podman-auto-update.timer` off. Nothing updates. When you
  are ready, run `sudo podman auto-update`: that is the approval, with the same
  healthcheck and the same rollback. Podman updates every labeled container on
  the machine when it runs, not just these, and can't be told to skip one, so a
  box that has to run the timer for other containers can't also hold these.
- **A window.** `update-window.conf` is a drop-in for the
  timer that says when it may fire, such as Sunday at 03:00, instead of the
  default of daily at midnight:

  ```sh
  sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/podman-auto-update.timer.d
  sudo cp update-window.conf /etc/systemd/system/podman-auto-update.timer.d/
  sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart podman-auto-update.timer
  ```

The Edge Relay is different on one count: a Gateway can approve its update
from the fleet screen, because a relay already listens for commands from the
Gateway it forwards to. IoT, Edge, and Gateway have no such channel to reach them,
and building one would put a "restart this box" button on a web UI for the sake
of a feature that `sudo podman auto-update` already is. See
[EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/#updating-a-relay) for the relay's
hold, and `edge-relay-hold.conf`.

## What the Gateway sees

`GET /api/status` on any of the three says its `version`, and its `imageDigest`
when the unit said (it does, before every start). An Edge or Gateway that has
edge publish on is a Sparkplug node like a relay, and puts the same two in
every birth, so a Gateway that has it in its fleet list shows the version and
digest and logs the change when an auto-update moves it
([FLEET.md](/gateway/fleet/)). IoT has no upstream, so its digest is on its
own `/api/status` and nowhere else.

## Under Helm

A pod can't replace itself, so there is no unattended update for the charts:
`helm upgrade` is the update, and the chart's `image.tag` defaults to its
`appVersion`, which is the release.
